title: Resource Contention in Production

sections.title: Synchronous Dependencies on the Request Path
Shared Pools and Fleet-Wide Session Limits
Open-Loop Load Testing and Flag Rollback

html:
Much of your day as an engineer is spent modifying applications that already serve customers, and many of those modifications are relatively small. A ticket comes up during a sprint. The product manager wants to add a “Recommended for you” row to every product page, hoping that showing customers related items will encourage additional purchases.

The implementation seems straightforward. Another team already runs a Recommendation Service for the home page, so you add a call to that service in the product-page handler and write a unit test that substitutes a predefined response for the actual service call. The test passes, the reviewer approves the pull request, and the change is ready for deployment.

What the test confirmed is that the handler builds the page correctly when a recommendation comes back. The predefined response arrived in a fraction of a millisecond and never touched a database, so the test revealed nothing about the work the production service does for each request. Once the change is deployed, every product page calls Recommendation Service, and each of those calls checks out a connection from a database pool that the home page and checkout already share. Because the pull request contained no code that touched that pool, the reviewer had no reason to look at it.

Baodium’s product-page team made this very change when it added personalized recommendations to the marketplace. The suggestions were correct in testing, but the release plan had no estimate of how many extra lookups the shared database would receive. The handler also waited for recommendations before returning the product, even though a customer could browse and buy without them.

Synchronous Dependencies on the Request Path

Before the change, Product Page Service fetched product details from Catalog Service and used them to build the response (Figure Figure).

The new handler added a second call and waited for it before building the page.

def get_product_page(user_id, product_id):
    product = catalog_service.fetch(product_id)
    recs = recommendation_service.get(user_id, product_id)
    return build_response(product, recs)

Let’s look at the order of those three lines. Because the recommendation call sits between fetching the product and building the response, any slow lookup now delays the whole page.

The product manager had asked for personalization as an addition to the page, but the code made every page wait for it, turning an optional feature into a required one. No configuration file or design document recorded that decision. It existed only in the order of three lines of code, and the review had checked whether those lines were correct rather than what they would wait for.

The team enabled the feature for one percent of eligible customers. A feature-flag service published the rollout percentage, and each Product Page instance checked the flag before making the recommendation call.1 One percent of customers is not necessarily one percent of page requests, because some customers browse far more than others, and the release owner was watching the customer percentage rather than the lookup rate.

The release owner raised the percentage in stages, and for the first few stages the latency dashboard showed no change. Then the slowest pages began to take longer while the median barely changed, and seventeen minutes after the first increase a customer-facing latency alert fired.

Diagnosing Connection-Pool Saturation

The on-call engineer started with the recommendation queries. Their execution times matched the measurements taken before the release, which made slow Structured Query Language (SQL) statements an unlikely cause of the page delays. The timings could not rule out every database problem, since lock waits or a handful of slow queries can hide inside an average, but they pointed the engineer toward the part of a request that happens before any query runs.

That part is the connection pool. Opening a database connection takes a network handshake and authentication, which is too slow to repeat for every request. Instead, an application maintains a set of open connections and lends one to each request while that request talks to the database. That set is the connection pool. Some pools open their connections at startup and others create them on demand, but every pool enforces a configured maximum.

A bank branch with forty tellers works the same way. Each transaction might take only a minute, but a customer who arrives when every teller is busy waits in line before that minute even starts, and it is the wait in line that makes the visit slow.

Each Recommendation Service instance allowed at most 40 connections. The engineer pulled up the pool’s readout from an affected instance (Listing Listing).2

assigned_connections    40
idle_connections        0
pending_acquisitions    80
acquire_p99             600 ms
query_p99               near baseline
occupancy_mean          70 ms

All 40 connections were assigned, and another 80 requests were waiting for one. The acquire_p99 line is the 99th percentile, usually written p99, and it says that 99 percent of connection acquisitions finished within 600 milliseconds and one percent took longer. At about 400 lookups a second, that is roughly four lookups every second waiting more than half a second before their SQL even started, on top of the many shorter waits elsewhere in the queue.

Those requests had not reached the database yet, so their wait never appeared in the query timings, which is why the timings alone gave no warning. The pages were slow because their recommendation calls were queuing for a connection.

Acquisition, Execution, and Occupancy

The readout was useful because the service measured three intervals separately.

Acquisition

is the time a request waits to receive a connection.

Execution

is the time a single SQL statement takes once it runs.

Occupancy

is the whole time a request has the connection, including any work it does between statements.

Each combination of these numbers points an investigation in a different direction. Long acquisition with normal execution means requests are queuing for the pool. The next questions are about demand, bursts, and how long each request occupies its connection. Fast acquisition with slow execution puts the database itself under suspicion, with its query plans, locks, and disk.

Suppose the team had recorded only total request time. Both situations would have produced the same graph, and the fix most people try first, tuning the queries, would have left the queue in place. Chapter 8 shows how to collect these measurements across a whole request path, including the attempts that time out before they ever receive a connection.

Shared Pools and Fleet-Wide Session Limits

Product pages produced most of the new lookups, but home-page and checkout requests drew from the same pool and waited in the same line. That is how an optional feature on the product page began to slow checkout, the page the business could least afford to slow.

Two fixes came up during the incident call. A bigger pool would let more lookups run concurrently, and more Recommendation Service instances would spread the traffic. Both sounded reasonable, and both would open more database sessions.

Because each instance has its own pool, twenty instances allowed forty connections each could open 800 sessions against one PostgreSQL server. Two separate limits sit behind that number. PostgreSQL caps how many sessions it accepts, and, independently, the server has a fixed amount of central processing unit (CPU) time, memory, and disk for running the queries those sessions send. A database that accepts 800 sessions can still slow down badly when 800 queries run concurrently.

The engineers on the call did not know how much of either limit belonged to Recommendation Service. Raising the pool size or the number of instances risked turning a slow feature into a database outage.

Decision review

Which mitigation restores the required page?

Personalization has reached full exposure. The pool has 40 assigned connections, 80 pending acquisitions, and an acquisition p99 of 600 ms. SQL latency is near baseline. The release owner can disable personalization, increase the connection pool, or add replicas.

Increase each pool from 40 to 80 connections.

Add four Recommendation Service replicas.

Disable personalization while the team investigates.

The third option removes the optional demand without introducing more sessions on a database whose limits have not been tested at that level. Increasing pool size or replica total could be appropriate later, after the database’s session limit and throughput have been measured. The team disabled personalization, then designed a bounded lookup and measured both page completion and recommendation delivery during its next rollout.

Optional Dependencies With Bounded Admission

Turning the flag off brought product pages back, but the product manager still wanted the feature. Before comparing designs, the team wrote down three requirements.

  1. A product page always returns the product within its latency objective.

  2. Recommendations appear on at least 95 percent of eligible pages during peak traffic.

  3. The page never waits in a queue for recommendations.

The second requirement ruled out the easy designs. A design that protected latency by dropping recommendations on most pages would meet the latency objective and still fail the product goal.

With those requirements written down, the team compared three designs (Table Table).

Parallel calls would shorten the page but leave the database load unchanged, and that load had caused the incident. Precomputation would remove most live queries, and Chapter 5 examines it in detail, but it needed a new refresh pipeline and storage that the team could not build before the next promotion.

A bounded lookup retained the live design and capped two things, how many lookups each instance could run and how long the page would wait.3 The open question was whether those caps could still deliver recommendations on 95 percent of pages. Only a load test could settle that.

Choosing the Limits

Two settings define the bounded lookup, and the team derived each one from a measurement.

The concurrency limit came from the database side. The database team allocated Recommendation Service a share of sessions and query capacity. The team divided that share across the expected number of instances, reserved room for one instance to fail, and arrived at 16 concurrent recommendation calls per Product Page instance.

The time budget came from the page side. The product page had a latency objective. Building and sending the response took a measured slice of it, and about 150 milliseconds were left for optional work. Listing Listing records both settings where the handler can read them.

import threading

# From the tested per-instance allocation (Chapter 2).
REC_CONCURRENCY = 16
# Optional-work share of the page latency objective.
REC_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 0.15
# Time reserved for building and sending the response.
RENDER_RESERVE_SECONDS = 0.05

rec_slots = threading.BoundedSemaphore(REC_CONCURRENCY)
def page(user_id, product_id, deadline):
    product = catalog_service.fetch(product_id)
    budget = min(REC_TIMEOUT_SECONDS,
                 deadline.remaining_seconds() - RENDER_RESERVE_SECONDS)
    if budget <= 0 or not rec_slots.acquire(blocking=False):
        metrics.rec_skipped.inc()
        return build_response(product, recommendations=[])
    try:
        recs = recommendation_service.get(
            user_id, product_id, timeout=budget)
    except (TimeoutError, ServiceUnavailable):
        metrics.rec_failed.inc()
        recs = []
    finally:
        rec_slots.release()
    return build_response(product, recommendations=recs)

Let’s walk through the handler. It fetches the product first, because there is no page without it. It then works out how much time it can spend on recommendations, taking the smaller of the fixed 150-millisecond budget and whatever is left of the page’s deadline once time is set aside to render the response.

If there is no time left, or all 16 slots are taken, the page goes out without a recommendation row and a counter records the skip. This is the line that stops a slow Recommendation Service from building a queue inside the product page. When a slot is free, the call runs with the computed budget. A timeout or an unavailable service gives the customer an empty row instead of an error page, and bumps a counter so the team can see how often it happens. The finally block releases the slot no matter how the call ends, so a failure can never leak capacity.

The handler catches only the failures the team expected, a timeout and an unavailable service. Any other exception, such as a bug in the recommendation client, still reaches the application’s error handling and shows up in the error rate, where an engineer will see it. Catching every exception would hide defects behind an empty row.

Before you copy this pattern, know its two limits. When the handler stops waiting, Recommendation Service may still be working on the request, so the caller’s timeout does not by itself free a database connection. And rec_slots only limits one instance. Sixteen slots on each of twenty instances still allow 320 lookups across the fleet, and that number is safe only because the team derived it from the fleet’s database allocation. Chapter 4 covers deadlines and cancellation, and Chapter 9 turns per-instance limits into limits shared across a fleet.

Open-Loop Load Testing and Flag Rollback

The one-percent stage of the first rollout had sent too little traffic to reveal the pool limit. Before raising exposure again, the team ran a load test at the expected peak rate. They used an open-loop test, which sends new requests on a fixed schedule however slowly the service responds.

A test that waits for each response before sending the next one lowers its own load as the service slows, so it can hide the overload it is meant to find.4 Chapter 2 explains how to read the results of such a test and turn them into an admission limit.

The test ran at peak traffic, with uneven routing between instances, and again with one instance removed. Even in the worst case, product pages met their latency objective and connection acquisition took under ten milliseconds. Recommendations appeared on 97 percent of eligible pages, above the 95 percent target. Those results approved the two settings in Listing Listing and a rollout plan that raised exposure in stages, with the release owner watching recommendation lookups per instance rather than customer percentages.

The team also rehearsed turning the feature off. A flag change takes effect only after every instance has received the new setting, and requests already waiting for connections still finish or time out. The rehearsal measured both delays. If the flag ever had to be switched off during another incident, the release owner would know how long relief would take. Chapter 10 turns observations like these into release gates.

Summary

If you take one lesson from this chapter, make it this one. Every call you add to a request path borrows something that other requests also need, and the review that approves the code rarely shows what that is.

Think back to the feature request that opened the chapter. The developer added a recommendation call, tested it against a stub, and released a feature the product team wanted. The review never saw the extra demand that call would place on a database pool that checkout and the home page already depended on.

The investigation worked because the team measured the right part of the request. The SQL queries ran as fast as before. The time went into waiting for a connection. Once the engineers knew where the delay occurred, they wrote down what the page needed, compared designs against those requirements, and chose limits from measurements of the database and the page budget.

You will face the same decision when you add an entitlement check to a SaaS application, call an external fraud service, or fetch profile data from another team’s API. Each new call has to fit within the resources the application already shares and the promises it already makes to its users. Here, the team found the problem in production. Chapter 2 takes us back to the design review, where we can estimate that demand before the change reaches customers.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & The live lookup can meet the page-latency objective and the recommendation-delivery target at a tested per-instance attempt rate.
Condition that tests it & Increasing feature exposure increases recommendation calls per instance.
Constraint or invariant & Per-instance connection pools share one database. The resource budget includes existing callers and the new product-page workload.
Evidence and uncertainty & The initial canary used a small fraction of the connection demand expected at full exposure. Acquisition waits increased when all connections were assigned.

Still unknown: the acceptable per-instance attempt rate under uneven routing, longer occupancy, or the loss of a service instance.
Signal and evaluation window & Compare connection acquisition, occupancy, and page latency with the pre-release baseline at each exposure step.
Control and decision & Limit exposure to the validated range. Reconsider live computation if recommendation delivery misses its target at that rate.
Owner and review trigger & The Recommendation Service owner provides load-test and recovery results. The release owner approves exposure against the recorded thresholds. Review after the test condition occurs or before expanding exposure.

  1. LaunchDarkly and Unleash are examples of feature-flag systems. Chapter 10 shows how a flag selects a rollout cohort, how a new setting reaches every instance, and how a flag is disabled during an incident.↩︎

  2. A readout here means a point-in-time snapshot of the pool’s own counters and timings, as reported by the connection-pool library’s metrics or diagnostic endpoint. Field names differ between libraries, so the labels in this example are illustrative.↩︎

  3. A bounded lookup is a dependency call with two limits, a time budget that bounds how long the caller waits and an admission limit that bounds how many calls may be in flight concurrently. Chapter 4 discusses what happens when the caller stops waiting but the remote work carries on.↩︎

  4. In k6, the constant-arrival-rate executor schedules iterations at a fixed rate. Its dropped_iterations metric reports iterations that could not start.↩︎
